sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Trastuzumab Deruxtecan (T-DXd / Enhertu)
sectionToMerge.intro: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd, sold as Enhertu) is a targeted antibody-drug conjugate used for certain HER2-expressing cancers. These FAQs explain who may be eligible, how treatment works, and what patients and caregivers can expect.

items.a: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), sold as Enhertu, is a targeted antibody-drug conjugate used mainly for HER2-positive and HER2-low cancers. It combines a HER2-targeting antibody with a chemotherapy payload delivered directly to cancer cells. It is given as an intravenous infusion under specialist supervision. Suitability depends on cancer type, HER2 status, previous treatment, and overall health, and should be confirmed by a qualified oncology team.

items.q: How does trastuzumab deruxtecan work in the body?
items.a: T-DXd works by attaching to HER2 proteins on cancer cells and releasing a chemotherapy payload inside them. The antibody portion finds HER2-expressing cells, and once inside, the linked drug damages the cancer cell's DNA. It may also affect nearby tumor cells through a bystander effect. Because it targets HER2, response can depend on how much HER2 a tumor expresses, which is assessed through laboratory testing of tumor tissue.

items.q: Which cancers is Enhertu used to treat?
items.a: Enhertu is approved for several HER2-related cancers, including HER2-positive and HER2-low breast cancer, HER2-positive gastric or gastroesophageal cancer, and certain HER2-mutant or HER2-expressing lung and other solid tumors. Approved uses vary by country and continue to evolve as new evidence emerges. Whether it applies to a specific diagnosis depends on cancer type, HER2 test results, and prior treatment, and should be reviewed by the treating oncology team.

items.q: What is the difference between HER2-positive and HER2-low cancer?
items.a: HER2-positive cancers strongly overexpress the HER2 protein, while HER2-low cancers show lower but still detectable HER2 levels on testing. This distinction matters because T-DXd has shown activity in both groups, expanding the number of patients who may be considered. HER2 status is determined through immunohistochemistry (IHC) and sometimes additional tests on tumor tissue. Accurate HER2 classification requires laboratory review and should guide treatment discussions with a specialist.

items.q: Who is eligible for trastuzumab deruxtecan?
items.a: Trastuzumab deruxtecan may be considered for patients whose tumors express HER2 and who meet specific clinical criteria. Eligibility depends on cancer type, stage, HER2 test results, previous treatments, organ function, and overall health. It is often used after other therapies, though approved settings vary. Final eligibility should be determined by a qualified oncology team after reviewing pathology, biomarker testing, imaging, and the patient's full medical history.

items.q: How is Enhertu given, and how often?
items.a: Enhertu is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, usually once every three weeks, in a hospital or specialized infusion center. The dose is calculated based on body weight, and each session is supervised by trained staff. Treatment continues as long as it is helping and side effects remain manageable. The exact schedule, number of cycles, and monitoring plan are decided by the treating oncology team based on individual response and tolerance.

items.q: What are the common side effects of trastuzumab deruxtecan?
items.a: Common side effects of T-DXd may include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, hair loss, low blood counts, and reduced appetite. Most side effects are managed with supportive medicines and dose adjustments. Reactions vary from person to person, and not everyone experiences the same symptoms. Patients should report new or worsening symptoms promptly. The oncology team monitors blood tests and overall health closely throughout treatment to manage side effects safely.

items.q: Is interstitial lung disease a risk with Enhertu?
items.a: Yes, interstitial lung disease (ILD), or lung inflammation, is an important potential risk with Enhertu and requires careful monitoring. Symptoms can include new cough, shortness of breath, or fever, and should be reported immediately. Doctors may use scans and lung function checks to watch for it. If ILD is suspected, treatment may be paused or stopped. Early detection is important, so close follow-up with the oncology team is essential.

items.q: What tests and reports are needed before starting T-DXd?
items.a: Before starting T-DXd, doctors typically need HER2 testing on tumor tissue, recent imaging scans, blood tests, and a review of previous treatments. A pathology report confirming HER2 status is essential, since eligibility depends on it. Heart and lung function may also be assessed because of possible side effects. Gathering complete and up-to-date medical records helps the oncology team confirm suitability and plan treatment safely and accurately.

items.q: How much does trastuzumab deruxtecan cost?
items.a: The cost of trastuzumab deruxtecan varies widely by country, hospital, dose, and number of cycles needed. As a newer targeted therapy, it can be expensive, and prices differ between healthcare systems and insurance arrangements. Final cost depends on diagnosis, treatment duration, supportive care, tests, and length of stay. Patients are encouraged to request a detailed estimate from the treating hospital and to explore insurance or assistance options where available.

Enhertu availability in India can vary over time and by hospital, as access to newer targeted therapies depends on regulatory approval, import status, and supply. Some major cancer centers may offer it for eligible patients. Availability, pricing, and approved uses can change, so it is best to confirm current access directly with a treating hospital or oncology team. Eligibility still depends on HER2 status and individual medical review.

Trastuzumab deruxtecan is approved and available in many countries, including the United States, several European nations, Japan, and others, though approved uses differ by region. Availability depends on local regulatory approval and hospital supply. Some patients travel abroad to access it where it is offered. Because approvals and availability change over time, patients should verify current options with hospitals or an oncology team before making treatment or travel decisions.

items.q: How can international patients access Enhertu?
items.a: International patients may access Enhertu by identifying hospitals that offer it and confirming eligibility through medical review. Access depends on HER2 status, hospital acceptance, availability, visa approval, and fitness to travel. Patients typically share pathology reports, imaging, and treatment history for assessment before travel. Costs, admission, and treatment acceptance are not guaranteed. Careful planning with the receiving hospital and treating team helps ensure a smooth and safe treatment journey.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for trastuzumab deruxtecan?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials continue to study trastuzumab deruxtecan in different cancers, stages, and treatment combinations. These trials may explore new uses or earlier treatment settings. Enrollment is not guaranteed and depends on strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, medical record review, and investigator assessment. Participation offers potential access to research treatment but does not guarantee benefit. Patients interested in trials should discuss options and eligibility with their oncology team.

items.q: What happens if T-DXd stops working?
items.a: If trastuzumab deruxtecan stops working, the oncology team may consider other treatment options based on cancer type, previous therapies, and current health. Alternatives can include different targeted drugs, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or clinical trials. Additional testing may help guide the next step. Every situation is different, and treatment decisions depend on individual factors. A specialist review helps determine the most appropriate next line of therapy for each patient.

items.q: Can T-DXd be combined with other cancer treatments?
items.a: Combining T-DXd with other cancer treatments is an active area of research, and some combinations are being studied in clinical trials. Whether it can be safely combined depends on cancer type, other therapies, and potential overlapping side effects. Standard use is often as a single targeted agent. Any combination approach should be guided by current evidence and decided by the treating oncology team based on the patient's specific situation.

items.q: How long does treatment with Enhertu usually last?
items.a: Treatment with Enhertu usually continues as long as it is helping control the cancer and side effects remain manageable. There is no fixed number of cycles for everyone; some patients receive it for many months. The oncology team reviews response through regular scans and blood tests, adjusting the plan as needed. Treatment duration depends on how the cancer responds and how well the patient tolerates therapy over time.

items.q: Do patients need to stay abroad for the full treatment course?
items.a: Not always; some international patients receive initial cycles abroad and continue treatment closer to home if the same therapy is available locally. Because Enhertu is often given every three weeks over an extended period, travel and follow-up planning are important. Continuity of care depends on local availability and coordination between hospitals. Patients should discuss follow-up arrangements and monitoring with both the treating and home oncology teams before starting.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with trastuzumab deruxtecan?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, HER2 status, previous treatment, and overall health. CancerFax does not guarantee hospital admission, treatment acceptance, or outcomes, and always defers to the treating medical team for final decisions.
